recipes.title: Vanilla Bean Panna Cotta with Berries
recipes.blurb: Barely set, wobbling, pure cream and vanilla with a bright berry sauce spooned over. Fifteen minutes of work and the fridge does everything else.

items: 2 1/4 tsp (7 g) unflavored powdered gelatin (one 1/4-oz packet)
1 vanilla bean, split and scraped (or 1 tbsp / 15 ml vanilla bean paste)
2 cups (280 g) strawberries, hulled and quartered (or mixed berries)

instructions.title: Bloom the gelatin
instructions.text: Sprinkle the gelatin evenly over the 3 tbsp (45 ml) cold water in a small bowl and let it sit undisturbed for 5 to 10 minutes. It will absorb the water and turn into a solid, wrinkled, applesauce-like mass — that is called blooming, and it is what lets the gelatin dissolve smoothly later. Sprinkle rather than dump, or you will get a dry lump in the middle that never hydrates.

instructions.title: Warm the cream
instructions.text: Combine the cream, milk, sugar, salt, vanilla seeds, and the empty pod in a saucepan over medium heat. Warm it, stirring to dissolve the sugar, until it reaches 175°F (80°C) — steam rising and small bubbles just forming around the rim. Do not let it boil; boiling changes the flavor of the cream and can weaken the gelatin's setting power.

instructions.title: Melt in the gelatin
instructions.text: Take the pan off the heat, add the bloomed gelatin, and whisk for 30 to 60 seconds until it has completely dissolved. Rub a little of the liquid between your fingers — if you feel any grains at all, keep whisking over low heat without boiling. Undissolved gelatin means a rubbery bottom layer and a soupy top.

instructions.title: Steep and strain
instructions.text: Cover the pan and let the mixture steep for 10 minutes to draw out more vanilla flavor, then remove the pod and pour everything through a fine-mesh sieve into a pitcher with a spout. Straining catches any stray gelatin bits and bits of pod. Stir gently for another minute so it cools slightly and the vanilla seeds stay suspended rather than sinking to the bottom.

instructions.title: Portion into glasses
instructions.text: Divide the mixture among six 6-oz (180 ml) glasses, ramekins, or small bowls — you have about 720 ml, so roughly 120 ml each, which fills them about two-thirds full. One packet of gelatin sets exactly this much liquid to a soft, spoonable wobble; stretch the same packet over more cream and you get a panna cotta that never quite firms up. If you plan to unmold them, lightly oil the ramekins first with a neutral oil on a paper towel. Serving in glasses is easier and looks lovely with the sauce on top, so there is no shame in skipping the unmolding.

instructions.title: Chill until set
instructions.text: Cool the glasses on the counter for 20 minutes, then cover loosely and refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight. Panna cotta sets slowly and gently; at 2 hours it will still be soupy in the center. It holds well in the fridge for 3 days, so this is a genuinely good make-ahead dessert.

instructions.title: Make the berry sauce
instructions.text: Toss half the strawberries with the sugar, lemon juice, and salt in a small saucepan and cook over medium heat for 5 to 7 minutes, until they break down and the liquid thickens slightly and coats a spoon. Take it off the heat and stir in the remaining raw berries so you get both a syrupy base and fresh, bright pieces. Cool completely before spooning it over the cold panna cotta.

instructions.title: Check the set
instructions.text: A properly set panna cotta wobbles noticeably when you shake the glass and holds the impression of a spoon without being firm or bouncy. If it is soupy after 6 hours, the gelatin was under-dissolved or the mixture boiled. If it is rubbery and springs back, there was too much gelatin — use 2 tsp next time.

instructions.title: Unmold, if you like
instructions.text: To unmold, dip a ramekin in hot tap water for 8 to 10 seconds, run a thin knife around the very edge, set an inverted plate on top, and flip. Give it one firm shake and it should drop with a soft sigh. If nothing happens after two attempts, dip it for another 5 seconds; too long in hot water and the outside melts to a puddle.

instructions.title: Serve cold
instructions.text: Spoon the cooled berry sauce over each panna cotta right before serving and finish with a few flakes of sea salt or a mint leaf. Serve cold, straight from the fridge, since it softens quickly at room temperature. Add the sauce at the last minute so the surface stays clean and the fruit stays bright.

tips: For a firmer panna cotta you can unmold confidently, increase the gelatin to 3 tsp (9 g). For a barely-there, spoonable texture served in glasses, 2 1/4 tsp (7 g) is right.
Vanilla bean paste is the best value here — it gives you the visible seeds and true vanilla flavor without buying a whole pod.
Infuse the cream with other flavors while it steeps: a wide strip of lemon peel, 2 tbsp (10 g) coffee beans, or a cinnamon stick all work beautifully.
Make it up to 3 days ahead and keep it covered in the fridge. Add the sauce only when you serve.
If you are avoiding gelatin, agar agar works but sets much firmer and needs to boil for 2 minutes — use 1 tsp (2 g) powdered agar for this quantity and expect a sliceable rather than wobbly texture.
recipes.keyTemp: Warm the cream mixture to 175°F (80°C) — steaming with small bubbles at the edge — and never let it boil, or the gelatin weakens. Chill at 40°F (4°C) or below for at least 4 hours until it wobbles but holds a spoon mark.
recipes.pairing: A glass of Prosecco or a cup of espresso, with extra berries on the side.

recipes.title: Churros with Thick Chocolate Sauce
recipes.blurb: Crisp ridged sticks rolled in cinnamon sugar, with a chocolate sauce thick enough to stand a churro in. Fried right, they are crackly outside and hollow-light inside.

items: 8 cups (1.9 L) neutral oil such as canola or peanut, for frying
6 oz (170 g) dark chocolate (60 to 70 percent), chopped

instructions.title: Set up before you start
instructions.text: Fit a large piping bag with a large closed star tip (Ateco 848 or a Wilton 1M), stand it in a tall glass, and line a sheet pan with paper towels. Mix the coating sugar and cinnamon in a wide shallow dish. Frying moves fast and the dough is easiest to pipe while warm, so having everything in place before you turn on the heat genuinely matters here.

instructions.title: Boil the liquid
instructions.text: Combine the water, butter, sugar, and salt in a medium saucepan over medium-high heat and bring it to a full rolling boil, stirring until the butter has completely melted. Do not let it simmer for long before adding the flour, because evaporation changes the water-to-flour ratio and the dough will come out stiff. Everything should hit the boil together.

instructions.title: Cook the paste
instructions.text: Dump in all the flour at once and stir hard with a wooden spoon until it forms a shaggy ball, then keep cooking over medium heat for 2 minutes, mashing and turning the dough against the pan. It will smooth out, pull cleanly from the sides, and leave a thin film on the bottom of the pan. That film is your signal — you are drying the dough so it can absorb the eggs.

instructions.title: Cool it before the eggs
instructions.text: Transfer the dough to a mixing bowl and beat it with a paddle or wooden spoon for 2 minutes to release steam, until it is warm rather than hot, about 140°F (60°C). Adding eggs to scalding dough scrambles them and ruins the texture. The dough should no longer steam heavily when you stop stirring.

instructions.title: Beat in the eggs
instructions.text: Add the eggs one at a time, beating until each is fully absorbed before adding the next, then beat in the vanilla. The dough will look slick and separated after each egg and then come back together — keep going, this always happens. Finished dough should be thick, glossy, and fall from the spoon in a slow V-shaped ribbon.

instructions.title: Make the chocolate sauce
instructions.text: Whisk the cornstarch into 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the milk in a small bowl, then heat the remaining milk, cream, and sugar in a small saucepan until steaming. Whisk in the cornstarch slurry and simmer 1 minute until slightly thickened, then take it off the heat, add the chopped chocolate and salt, and let it sit 2 minutes before whisking smooth. Spanish chocolate a la taza is meant to be thick enough to coat a churro heavily — keep it warm over the lowest heat.

instructions.title: Heat the oil precisely
instructions.text: Pour all 8 cups (1.9 L) of oil into a heavy 4-quart (3.8 L) Dutch oven or deep pot about 9 in (23 cm) across, which gives you the 2 in (5 cm) depth a churro needs to float rather than sit on the bottom, and heat it over medium to 360°F (182°C) on a clip-on thermometer. Use a wider pot and you will need noticeably more oil to reach that depth. Temperature is everything here: below 340°F (171°C) the churros absorb oil and go greasy, and above 375°F (190°C) they brown before the inside cooks and can split violently. Never fill the pot more than halfway with oil.

instructions.title: Fill the piping bag
instructions.text: Scrape the warm dough into the prepared piping bag and twist the top closed, pushing the dough down to eliminate air pockets. Trapped air causes the churro to burst in hot oil and spit at you. Work while the dough is still warm, since it stiffens considerably as it cools.

instructions.title: Pipe and fry in batches
instructions.text: Pipe 6-in (15 cm) lengths directly over the oil, snipping the dough free with kitchen scissors, and fry only 4 at a time so the oil temperature does not crash. Fry for 2 to 3 minutes per side, turning once with tongs or a spider, until they are deep golden brown all over. Pale churros are raw inside; you want a genuinely dark gold. Check the oil temperature between batches and let it recover to 360°F (182°C).

instructions.title: Drain and coat
instructions.text: Lift the churros out to the paper towels for 20 seconds only, then roll them in the cinnamon sugar while they are still hot and slightly oily. Waiting even a minute means the sugar will not stick. Do not let them sit on the towels long enough to steam, or the ridges soften and you lose the crackle.

instructions.title: Serve immediately
instructions.text: Pile the churros on a plate and serve at once with the warm chocolate for dipping. Churros are at their absolute best within 10 minutes of frying and are noticeably worse after 30 — this is a dessert you make while everyone hovers in the kitchen. Reheat any leftovers at 400°F (200°C) for 4 minutes to bring back some crispness.

instructions.title: Cool and store the oil safely
instructions.text: Turn off the heat and let the oil cool completely in the pot, at least 2 hours, before doing anything with it. Strain it through a coffee filter or fine sieve into a sealed jar and reuse it two or three times for sweets. Never pour hot oil, and never pour any oil down the drain.

tips: The closed star tip is not decorative — those deep ridges create surface area that crisps, and a round tip gives you a doughnut stick instead of a churro.
If your piping bag threatens to burst, use two bags doubled up or a sturdy canvas bag. This dough is thick and takes real hand strength to pipe.
For a make-ahead version, pipe the churros onto a parchment-lined tray, freeze solid, then fry straight from frozen at 350°F (177°C) for about 4 minutes per side.
Keep a lid nearby whenever you fry. If the oil ever smokes or catches, slide the lid on and turn off the heat — never use water.
Churros that split open in the oil usually mean the oil was too hot or there were air pockets in the bag. Drop the temperature by 10 degrees and press the dough down firmly next batch.
recipes.keyTemp: Fry in oil held at 360°F (182°C) — below 340°F (171°C) they turn greasy and above 375°F (190°C) they burn outside while raw inside. Cook 2 to 3 minutes per side until deep golden all over.
recipes.pairing: Thick hot chocolate for dipping, or strong coffee with a splash of milk.

recipes.title: No-Churn Vanilla Ice Cream
recipes.blurb: Two ingredients, no machine, no custard to cook — just whipped cream folded into condensed milk and frozen. It scoops like real ice cream and takes fifteen minutes of work.

items: 2 cups (480 ml) heavy cream, very cold
1 can (14 oz / 396 g) sweetened condensed milk, chilled
1 tbsp (15 ml) vanilla bean paste or 2 tsp (10 ml) vanilla extract
2 tbsp (30 ml) vodka or bourbon (optional, keeps it scoopable)
1 cup (170 g) mini chocolate chips or chopped chocolate
1/2 cup (150 g) strawberry jam or fruit puree, for swirling
1 cup (100 g) crushed cookies such as Oreos or shortbread
1/2 cup (120 ml) salted caramel sauce, for rippling

instructions.title: Chill your equipment
instructions.text: Put a large metal mixing bowl and the beaters in the freezer for 15 minutes before you start, and keep the cream in the fridge until the second you need it. Cream whips faster, higher, and more stably when everything is cold, because the fat globules stay firm enough to trap air. Warm cream can take twice as long and never reaches the same volume.

instructions.title: Mix the sweet base
instructions.text: In a separate medium bowl, whisk the sweetened condensed milk with the vanilla, salt, and vodka if using until completely smooth. Doing this first means you are not stirring a thick sticky liquid into delicate whipped cream later. The salt matters more than it sounds — without it, this reads as flatly sweet.

instructions.title: Whip the cream to stiff peaks
instructions.text: Whip the cold cream in the chilled bowl on medium-high for 2 to 3 minutes, until it holds stiff peaks that stand straight up when you lift the beaters. Stiff rather than soft peaks are essential here, since the whipped air is the only thing standing between you and a block of frozen milk. Stop the moment it looks thick and matte; a few seconds more and it turns grainy and starts becoming butter.

instructions.title: Lighten the base
instructions.text: Scoop about a cup of the whipped cream into the condensed milk mixture and stir it in without any care for deflating it. This sacrificial cup loosens the dense base so the rest folds in with far fewer strokes. It is a small step that saves you a lot of lost volume.

instructions.title: Fold the rest together
instructions.text: Add the lightened base back to the whipped cream in two additions, folding with a spatula — cut down the center, sweep along the bottom, and lift over the top, rotating the bowl a quarter turn each time. Stop as soon as the color is uniform with no white or yellow streaks, about 20 folds. Stirring instead of folding knocks the air out and gives you a hard, icy result.

instructions.title: Add your mix-ins
instructions.text: Fold in solid add-ins like chocolate chips or crushed cookies with a few final strokes. For a swirl of jam or caramel, layer the base into the pan in thirds and dollop the sauce between layers, then drag a butter knife through it two or three times only. Over-swirling turns a beautiful ribbon into a muddy pink-brown blur.

instructions.title: Transfer and cover
instructions.text: Scrape the mixture into a 9x5-in (23x13 cm) metal loaf pan or a 1 1/2-quart (1.4 L) container and smooth the top. Press a piece of plastic wrap directly onto the surface before putting on a lid. Direct contact keeps air off the surface, and air is what forms those crunchy ice crystals on top of long-stored ice cream.

instructions.title: Freeze until firm
instructions.text: Freeze for at least 6 hours, ideally overnight, on a flat freezer shelf toward the back where the temperature is most stable, ideally 0°F (minus 18°C). It will look set at 3 hours but the center will still be soft and it will not scoop cleanly. A metal pan freezes faster and more evenly than glass or plastic.

instructions.title: Temper before scooping
instructions.text: Take the container out and let it sit on the counter for 5 minutes before serving. Ice cream scoops best around 10°F (minus 12°C), and straight from a cold freezer it can be hard enough to bend a spoon. Dip your scoop in hot water and shake off the drops between scoops for clean round balls.

instructions.title: Store it well
instructions.text: Keep it frozen for up to 2 weeks with the plastic pressed back onto the surface after each serving. The optional 2 tbsp (30 ml) of vodka lowers the freezing point just enough to keep it soft and scoopable in week two without any taste of alcohol. Beyond two weeks, freezer burn starts to win.

tips: Do not substitute evaporated milk for sweetened condensed milk. They sound similar and are completely different products; evaporated milk has no sugar and will freeze rock hard.
Coffee version: whisk 2 tbsp (10 g) instant espresso powder into the condensed milk. Chocolate version: whisk in 1/3 cup (28 g) cocoa powder and 2 tbsp (30 ml) hot water first to make a smooth paste.
This is the ideal thing to make with kids or on a hot day when you do not want the oven on at all — no cooking of any kind.
If your finished ice cream is icy rather than creamy, the cream was underwhipped or overfolded. Both mistakes remove the air that makes this work.
A metal loaf pan chilled in the freezer beforehand shortens the freeze time by nearly an hour.
recipes.keyTemp: No cooking required. Freeze at 0°F (minus 18°C) for at least 6 hours until firm, then let it sit 5 minutes at room temperature so it scoops at about 10°F (minus 12°C).
recipes.pairing: Warm brownies or a slice of peach cobbler, with hot fudge if you have it.

recipes.title: Peach Cobbler with Buttermilk Biscuits
recipes.blurb: Jammy peaches bubbling under craggy buttermilk biscuits with crunchy sugar tops. It is the easiest good fruit dessert there is, and it is even better with ice cream melting into it.

items: 3 lb (1.4 kg) ripe peaches (about 8 medium), sliced 1/2 in thick, roughly 8 cups
2 tbsp (25 g) packed light brown sugar
6 tbsp (85 g) cold unsalted butter, cut into 1/2-in cubes
2 tbsp (25 g) turbinado or coarse sugar, for sprinkling

instructions.title: Heat the oven and pick your dish
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) with a rack in the center and set a foil-lined sheet pan on the rack below to catch drips. Use a 9x13-in (23x33 cm) baking dish or a 12-in (30 cm) cast iron skillet. Cobbler almost always bubbles over, and cleaning burnt sugar off the oven floor is a genuinely miserable job.

instructions.title: Peel the peaches easily
instructions.text: If the skins bother you, score a small X in the bottom of each peach, drop them into boiling water for 45 seconds, then straight into ice water — the skins will slip right off with your fingers. Ripe peaches should smell sweet at the stem and give slightly under gentle pressure. You can absolutely leave the skins on; they soften in the oven and add color.

instructions.title: Toss the filling
instructions.text: In a large bowl, toss the sliced peaches with both sugars, the cornstarch, lemon juice, cinnamon, salt, and vanilla until every slice is coated and no dry cornstarch remains. Let it sit for 10 minutes while you make the biscuits so the juices start to draw out and the starch hydrates. The lemon keeps the peaches tasting like fruit rather than just sweet.

instructions.title: Whisk the biscuit dry mix
instructions.text: In a separate bowl, whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt together for 15 seconds. Baking powder clumps in the box and an unmixed clump means one biscuit with a bitter yellow center. This mixture can be made ahead and kept in the fridge.

instructions.title: Cut in cold butter
instructions.text: Add the cold butter cubes and rub them into the flour with your fingertips or cut them in with a pastry blender until the largest pieces are the size of small peas. Work quickly and stop while you can still see distinct butter — those pieces steam in the oven and create the flaky layers. If your kitchen is warm, pop the bowl in the freezer for 10 minutes.

instructions.title: Add the buttermilk
instructions.text: Pour in the cold buttermilk and stir with a fork just until a shaggy, sticky dough forms with no dry patches, about 12 strokes. It should look rough and lumpy, not smooth — this is a drop biscuit dough, not a kneaded one. Overmixing gives you dense, tough biscuits instead of tender craggy ones.

instructions.title: Fill the dish
instructions.text: Pour the peaches and all their juices into the baking dish and spread them into an even layer. Do not drain the juice; the cornstarch needs that liquid to thicken into a glossy sauce. The dish will look very full, which is right, since the fruit collapses considerably as it bakes.

instructions.title: Drop the biscuits
instructions.text: Scoop the dough into 8 or 9 rough mounds of about 1/4 cup (60 g) each — the batch weighs roughly 520 g, so do not try to stretch it to a dozen — and drop them over the fruit, leaving gaps between them. Those gaps let steam escape so the fruit thickens instead of steaming the biscuit bottoms into paste. Sprinkle the turbinado sugar generously over every biscuit top.

instructions.title: Bake until bubbling
instructions.text: Bake for 40 to 50 minutes, until the biscuits are deep golden brown and the fruit is bubbling thickly around the edges and in the center. Fast, watery bubbling means the cornstarch has not activated yet, so keep going. The biscuits are done when their centers read 200 to 205°F (93 to 96°C), or when a skewer inserted into one comes out clean.

instructions.title: Rest before serving
instructions.text: Set the dish on a rack and let it rest for 20 to 30 minutes before serving. The filling thickens dramatically as it cools, and served straight from the oven it will be soupy and lava hot. Warm, not hot, is the sweet spot — serve it with cold vanilla ice cream so it melts into the juices.

tips: Out of season, use 3 lb (1.4 kg) frozen sliced peaches straight from the freezer without thawing and add 1 extra tbsp (8 g) cornstarch plus 10 minutes of bake time.
No buttermilk? Stir 2 tsp (10 ml) lemon juice into 3/4 cup (180 ml) milk and let it stand 10 minutes. The acid is what reacts with the baking powder for a tall, tender biscuit.
Cobbler is best the day it is made but keeps 2 days covered in the fridge. Reheat at 350°F (175°C) for 15 minutes to bring the biscuit tops back to life.
Underripe hard peaches will not soften enough in the oven. Ripen them on the counter in a paper bag for a day or two first.
The same recipe works with blackberries, plums, or a mix of peaches and berries. Keep the total fruit at about 8 cups and adjust the sugar by how sweet the fruit tastes raw.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 40 to 50 minutes until the filling bubbles thickly and the biscuit centers read 200 to 205°F (93 to 96°C). Rest 20 to 30 minutes so the cornstarch sets.
recipes.pairing: A big scoop of vanilla ice cream, and sweet iced tea on the porch.

recipes.title: Lemon Bars with Shortbread Crust
recipes.blurb: A thick, tart lemon curd layer set over buttery shortbread, cut into squares and dusted with powdered sugar. Sharp enough to make you sit up, rich enough to feel like a real dessert.

items: 1 cup (226 g) unsalted butter, at room temperature
2 tbsp (12 g) finely grated lemon zest (from about 4 lemons)
1 cup (240 ml) fresh lemon juice (from about 6 lemons)
2 tbsp (15 g) powdered sugar, for dusting

instructions.title: Line the pan
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the center. Line a 9x13-in (23x33 cm) metal baking pan with a parchment sling that overhangs the two long sides by 2 in (5 cm), then lightly butter the short ends. The sling is how you get the whole slab out in one piece for clean cutting; digging bars out of a pan destroys the first row every time.

instructions.title: Cream the shortbread
instructions.text: Beat the room-temperature butter and granulated sugar with a paddle attachment on medium for 2 minutes until light and fluffy, scraping the bowl once. Add the flour and salt and mix on low just until a soft, crumbly dough forms that holds together when pressed. Stop as soon as it comes together — overworked shortbread bakes up hard rather than tender and sandy.

instructions.title: Press and chill
instructions.text: Dump the dough into the lined pan and press it into an even layer with your fingers, then smooth it flat with the bottom of a measuring cup, building a slight 1/4-in (6 mm) lip up the sides. An even thickness bakes evenly; thin patches burn while thick ones stay raw. Chill the pressed crust in the freezer for 15 minutes so the butter is cold going into the oven.

instructions.title: Bake the crust fully
instructions.text: Bake the crust for 20 to 25 minutes, until it is uniformly light golden brown and set to the touch, not pale and soft. A fully baked crust is what keeps the bottom crisp under a wet filling — pulled early, it goes soggy overnight. Leave the oven on and start the filling while the crust bakes.

instructions.title: Zest before juicing
instructions.text: Zest the lemons with a microplane before you cut them, taking only the yellow and none of the white pith, which is bitter. Then roll each lemon firmly under your palm on the counter before juicing to break the membranes and get significantly more juice out. You need a full 1 cup (240 ml) of juice, so buy an extra lemon or two for insurance.

instructions.title: Whisk the filling
instructions.text: Whisk the eggs and sugar together in a large bowl for 1 minute until smooth and pale, then whisk in the zest, lemon juice, flour, and salt until completely lump-free. Whisk gently rather than beating air into it, since foam bakes into a pale crust on top of the bars. Let the mixture rest 2 minutes and skim any foam that rises.

instructions.title: Pour onto the hot crust
instructions.text: Pour the filling directly over the hot crust as soon as it comes out of the oven, right in the pan on the oven rack if you can manage it safely. The hot surface immediately begins setting the bottom of the curd, which is what prevents that thin gummy layer between crust and filling. Pour slowly and evenly across the whole surface.

instructions.title: Bake until just set
instructions.text: Bake for 30 to 35 minutes, until the filling is set from edge to center and only the middle 2 in (5 cm) has a very slight jiggle when you nudge the pan. The surface should look matte with a faint pale skin and should not brown. An instant-read thermometer in the center should read about 175°F (79°C); above 185°F (85°C) the eggs curdle and weep.

instructions.title: Cool completely
instructions.text: Cool the pan on a wire rack to room temperature, about 1 hour. The curd continues to firm as it cools and cutting it warm gives you a shattered mess. Do not cover it while it is warm — trapped steam condenses on the surface and makes it sticky.

instructions.title: Chill before cutting
instructions.text: Refrigerate the cooled pan, uncovered, for at least 1 hour or up to overnight. A cold slab cuts into crisp-edged squares that hold their shape, while a room-temperature one drags and smears. Then lift out the slab by the sling onto a cutting board.

instructions.title: Cut and dust
instructions.text: Cut a 4 by 4 grid with a long sharp knife, wiping the blade clean with a hot damp towel between every cut. Dust with powdered sugar through a fine sieve immediately before serving, not before storing — the sugar dissolves into the moist curd within an hour and disappears. Serve cold or at cool room temperature.

tips: Use only fresh lemon juice. Bottled juice has a dull, slightly metallic taste that is impossible to hide when it is the main flavor of the dish.
Bars keep 4 days in an airtight container in the fridge with parchment between the layers. They also freeze up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge and re-dust with sugar.
If the filling weeps a little liquid after chilling, it was slightly overbaked. Blot gently with a paper towel before dusting and no one will know.
For lime bars, substitute the same volume of fresh lime juice and zest. For a Meyer lemon version, cut the sugar to 2 cups (400 g) since they are much sweeter.
Make the crust dough up to 3 days ahead and keep it pressed in the pan, wrapped, in the fridge. It bakes straight from cold with no changes.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake the crust at 350°F (175°C) for 20 to 25 minutes until golden, then bake the filling 30 to 35 minutes until the center reads about 175°F (79°C) and barely jiggles; past 185°F (85°C) the custard curdles.
recipes.pairing: A pot of Earl Grey, or a glass of Prosecco on a warm afternoon.
